1142.title: The laborer who was Shiva
1142.hook: Shiva hires out as a lazy laborer in Madurai, takes a king's cane, and every being feels the blow
1142.tomorrow: a minister carrying a king's gold meets a teacher under a tree.
1142.howItsDone: Madurai's temple tradition tells and celebrates Shiva's sacred games, including the day he carried earth for an old woman's puttu; students of Kashmir Shaivism study the Shiva Sutras line by line with a commentary.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FORTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a thread of the Shiva Sutras said wonder marks the stages of yoga. Today the same book builds a theater, and a story from Madurai walks onto its stage.
screen: `WONDER MARKS THE WAY.` · `TODAY: A THEATER, AND A LABORER.`

segments.voice: The river Vaigai has burst its banks at Madurai, and the king orders every household to send someone to carry earth to the breach. An old woman named Vandi sells steamed rice cakes, puttu, and every morning she offers the first one to Shiva. She has no son, no husband, no one to send. Then a young laborer turns up at her door. I'll do your share, he says, and you can pay me in puttu. He eats the cakes. And then he doesn't work.
screen: `THE RIVER BREAKS ITS BANKS.` → `AN OLD WOMAN WITH NO ONE TO SEND.` → `A LABORER, PAID IN PUTTU.`

segments.voice: This story comes from the Tamil temple tradition of Madurai, one of Shiva's sacred games. The laborer sings. He dances. He naps under a tree. Every other stretch of the bank rises, and Vandi's stays open. The king comes to inspect, sees the gap and the sleeping laborer, and strikes him across the back with his cane. And the blow lands on everyone. The king feels it on his own back. So does every worker on the bank, every creature in the land. The laborer tips one basket of earth into the breach, the bank closes, and he's gone. Then the king understands whom he struck. Now set it beside the Shiva Sutras, from far-off Kashmir. Nartaka atma: the self is a dancer. The stage is the inner self. The spectators are the senses. Kashmir Shaivism teaches that there is one consciousness, and it is Shiva's, playing every part: the king, the old woman, the laborer, you. That's why one blow could land on everyone. It was always one back. Many teachers read the dancer line as a picture of someone awake: not someone who quits the roles, but someone who plays each one fully and never forgets who's dancing. Shiva played a lazy laborer so well that a king hit him, and never stopped being Shiva. Here's where it meets an ordinary day. You'll play a dozen parts before tonight: student, child, annoyed friend. Play them all the way. And the person across from you, the one you're tempted to strike, is played by the same one.
screen: `SHIVA'S SACRED GAMES, MADURAI.` · `THE BLOW LANDS ON EVERYONE.` · `NARTAKA ATMA: THE SELF IS A DANCER.` · `ONE CONSCIOUSNESS, EVERY PART.` · then, large: `IT WAS ALWAYS ONE BACK.`

segments.voice: Name a few parts you've already played today: the one who got up, the one who answered a message, the one who was short with someone, or kind. Let each one step onto the inner stage, take a bow and step off, and notice the one who's watching, who was there for every part. If you pray, offer the whole performance to Shiva with Om namah shivaya. If you don't, just rest as the one watching.
Nartaka atma. The self is a dancer: in Kashmir Shaivism, one consciousness, Shiva's, playing every part.

segments.voice: Your line: one consciousness plays every part. It was always one back. See you tomorrow.

1143.title: The teacher under the tree
1143.hook: a minister carrying a king's gold meets a teacher under a tree, and never buys the horses
1143.carry: the teacher is the way: gurur upayah
1143.tomorrow: who is the fierce one with the dog at Shiva's door?
1143.howItsDone: Students of Kashmir Shaivism learn the Shiva Sutras from a teacher, line by line; many Hindus honor their teachers by touching their feet, and on Guru Purnima, the full-moon day for teachers.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FORTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: one consciousness plays every part, even a lazy laborer who took a king's cane. Today, the man that flood came for, and how he found his teacher.
screen: `ONE CONSCIOUSNESS, EVERY PART.` · `TODAY: THE TEACHER.`

segments.voice: The Pandya king of Madurai gives his chief minister a fortune in gold and one job: ride to the coast and buy the finest horses. On the way, at a place called Tirupperunturai, the minister hears chanting. Under a tree sits a teacher, with students around him, perfectly calm. The minister gets down from his horse. He meant to stop for a moment. He falls at the teacher's feet instead, the teacher blesses him, and something in him opens. He never buys the horses.
screen: `A KING'S GOLD, FOR HORSES.` → `A TEACHER UNDER A TREE.` → `HE NEVER BUYS THE HORSES.`

segments.voice: The minister became Manikkavasagar, one of the great poet-saints of Tamil Shaivism; the name means the one whose words are gems. He spent the king's gold on a temple and on Shiva's devotees, and paid for it: the king had him punished, and in the Madurai telling, yesterday's flood and the laborer who took the cane came for his sake. And the teacher under the tree? Tradition says it was Shiva himself, come as a guru. Now the Shiva Sutras: gurur upayah. Guru is a teacher. Upaya is a means, the thing that gets you there. The teacher is the way. This book has said you are consciousness, that small knowing binds, that the self is a dancer who can forget who's dancing. If that's the problem, more information won't fix it. It's a habit of seeing, and habits change through someone who has seen. The commentator Kshemaraja reads the line more widely still: the guru is also Shiva's own grace, his power to reveal, working through a person. That's the teaching under a very Hindu habit. It's why students touch a teacher's feet, why many keep Guru Purnima, a full-moon day for honoring teachers, and why a mantra is traditionally received from a teacher, not copied off a page. Grace tends to arrive with a face. And the student still walks: Manikkavasagar still had to get down from his horse. So if something matters to you, a chant, a prayer, an instrument, find the person who can hand it over.
screen: `MANIKKAVASAGAR: WORDS LIKE GEMS.` · `THE GURU WAS SHIVA. GURUR UPAYAH.` · `A HABIT OF SEEING, HANDED ON.` · `SHIVA'S GRACE, THROUGH A PERSON.` · then, large: `THE TEACHER IS THE WAY.`

segments.voice: Do what many Hindus do for a teacher. Bring to mind someone who showed you a way: a parent at the stove, a coach, a teacher who stayed after class. Let their face come, put your palms together, and bow your head toward them, a silent thank-you. If you pray, thank Shiva for the grace that came through them. If you don't, the thank-you is enough.
Gurur upayah. The teacher is the way: in Kashmir Shaivism, the guru, and Shiva's grace working through one.

1144.title: Bhairava at the door
1144.hook: Brahma boasts, and in an instant a fierce form springs out of Shiva: Bhairava, who now guards Kashi
1144.carry: bhairava is the flash that cuts the ego
1144.tomorrow: Nani says Shiva's name fifty times while cooking. does that count?
1144.howItsDone: Pilgrims in Varanasi visit the temple of Kala Bhairava, the city's guardian, and many Shiva temples keep a shrine to Bhairava with his dog; students of the Shiva Sutras read udyamo bhairavah with a commentary and connect it to meditation.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FORTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the teacher is the way, and a minister who met Shiva under a tree. Today, Shiva's fiercest face, and a line in the Shiva Sutras that names him.
screen: `GURUR UPAYAH.` · `TODAY: THE ONE AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Brahma, the creator, is boasting. In the Shiva Purana's telling, he grows so proud that he speaks of Shiva with contempt, as if he himself were the source of everything. And in an instant, faster than an argument, a figure springs out of Shiva: dark, fierce, eyes blazing. Bhairava. He goes straight to Brahma and, with one fingernail, cuts off the head that boasted. Brahma had five heads. From that day, the story says, he has four.
screen: `BRAHMA BOASTS.` → `IN AN INSTANT, BHAIRAVA.` → `FIVE HEADS, THEN FOUR.`

segments.voice: The story keeps going. The skull sticks to Bhairava's hand. Even a god who cuts down pride has to answer for the cut, so Bhairava wanders the world as a beggar, the skull for his bowl, until he reaches Kashi, the city of Varanasi. There it falls from his hand. Shiva makes him Kashi's guardian, and pilgrims in Varanasi still visit Kala Bhairava; many Shiva temples keep a shrine to Bhairava too, a fierce figure with a dog. Many teachers read the fifth head as ahamkara, the ego, the I that boasts. Bhairava is Shiva's answer to it: not a lecture, a flash. Now the Shiva Sutras use his name: udyamo bhairavah. Udyama is an upsurge, a springing up. The upsurge is Bhairava. Commentators read it as the sudden flash of awareness, consciousness springing up all at once, not reasoned into step by step. In Kashmir Shaivism, Bhairava isn't only a fierce figure near the door. He's a name for consciousness itself, awake. And the flash, as in the story, cuts the boasting head: the little I that thought it was the center of everything. Here's how it meets an ordinary day. You're halfway through an argument, or a daydream, or a brag, and suddenly you see yourself doing it. That snap, before the next thought, isn't your failure. On this teaching, it's Bhairava at the door.
screen: `THE SKULL FALLS IN KASHI.` · `THE FIFTH HEAD: THE EGO.` · `UDYAMO BHAIRAVAH: THE UPSURGE.` · `CONSCIOUSNESS, AWAKE, IS BHAIRAVA.` · then, large: `THE FLASH THAT CUTS THE BOAST.`

segments.voice: Rest your attention on the breath, and when the mind wanders off, as it will, don't scold it. Pause in the noticing itself, that snap of being awake again, for one breath. Then return, and wait for the next one. If you pray, greet each return with Om namah shivaya, or with Bhairava's name. If you don't, let the snap be the whole practice.
Udyamo bhairavah. The upsurge is Bhairava: the sudden flash of awareness, Shiva's fierce form, cutting the boasting I.

segments.voice: Your line: Bhairava is the flash that cuts the ego. The snap of seeing yourself is the point, not the mistake. Until tomorrow.

1145.hook: a stranger writes down Manikkavasagar's songs at Chidambaram, and they open with Shiva's name

1145.howItsDone: Japa is a Hindu practice: repeating a mantra or divine name, often counted on a mala of 108 beads; Tamil Shaivas sing Manikkavasagar's Tiruvachakam in homes and temples, and many Hindus greet each other with a god's name.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FORTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhairava is the flash that cuts the ego, the guardian at Shiva's door. Today, our last day in the Shiva Sutras, and Manikkavasagar again, near the end of his road.
screen: `THE FLASH THAT CUTS THE BOAST.` · `LAST DAY IN THE SHIVA SUTRAS.`

segments.voice: Years after the tree and the flood, Manikkavasagar has walked from temple to temple, singing. He comes at last to Chidambaram, the city of the dancing Shiva. There, tradition says, a stranger asks him to recite all his songs, and writes them down on palm leaves as he speaks. The next morning the bundle is found on the temple step, signed: written by the Lord of the sacred hall. The stranger was Shiva. And the songs open with five syllables: namachivaya.
screen: `A STRANGER WRITES THE SONGS DOWN.` → `SIGNED: THE LORD OF THE SACRED HALL.` → `IT OPENS: NAMACHIVAYA.`

segments.voice: The book is the Tiruvachakam, the sacred utterance, and Tamil Shaivas still sing it in homes and temples. Its first song opens namachivaya vazhga: long live namah shivaya, the five-syllable mantra. When the priests asked what the songs meant, tradition says Manikkavasagar pointed to the dancing Shiva, walked into the shrine, and was not seen again. The meaning was him. That mantra is the heart of a practice called japa: repeating a divine name, slowly, with attention, often on a string of a hundred and eight beads. Om namah shivaya, again and again, until the name is the groove the mind runs in. Now the Shiva Sutras, in the book's last section: katha japah. Katha is talk, conversation. For the awakened yogi, his conversation is japa. Commentators explain: japa keeps awareness of Shiva alive, again and again. For someone who rests in that awareness all the time, there's nothing left to switch on. The lines around it say the same of the body, keeping it going is the vow, and of giving: the gift is knowledge of the self. That's how a poet's spoken words could become scripture: they already carried the name. And it's why so many Hindus greet each other with a god's name, Ram Ram, Jai Shri Krishna, Har Har Mahadev, and murmur Shiva, Shiva while they cook. Not every word is holy yet. The practice is to say the name so often that, one day, the talk itself is japa.
screen: `THE TIRUVACHAKAM, SUNG TODAY.` · `JAPA: THE NAME, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `KATHA JAPAH: TALK IS JAPA.` · `RAM RAM. HAR HAR MAHADEV.` · then, large: `TALK ITSELF BECOMES JAPA.`

segments.voice: Try japa the way it's done. Hold a mala if you have one, or count on the joints of your fingers, and say Om namah shivaya, softly or silently, eleven times, slowly enough to hear each syllable. Then let an ordinary thought come, and notice whether the name is still humming under it. If you don't pray, say the meaning instead: I bow to the auspicious one.
Katha japah. His conversation is japa: for one who rests in Shiva, ordinary talk already carries the name. That closes our time in the Shiva Sutras.

segments.voice: An old ritual book, the Shatapatha Brahmana, tells a frightening story. The creator, Prajapati, has fallen apart, worn out from making the world, and the gods have drifted away from him. Only one power stays inside him: Manyu, wrath. Prajapati weeps, his tears settle on that wrath, and it becomes Rudra: a hundred heads, a thousand eyes, a hundred quivers of arrows. The gods are terrified. What do you do with a god like that?
screen: `WRATH, AND A CREATOR'S TEARS.` → `RUDRA, A HUNDRED QUIVERS.` → `THE GODS ARE TERRIFIED.`

segments.voice: The gods say to one another: let's gather food for him, and calm him. So they offer him the hymn of the hundred Rudras, the Shatarudriya, and with it, the story says, he is appeased. That hymn is the Rudram, in the Krishna Yajur Veda. Listen to its first line: namaste rudra manyave. A bow to your anger, Rudra. Manyu, the very wrath he was made from. Then a bow to his arrow, his bow, his arms. It doesn't pretend the danger isn't there. It names it, and bows. Then it asks. Make your arrow kind. Look on us with your auspicious body. Unstring the bow; put the arrows away. The word for kind and auspicious there is shiva. So the hymn asks Rudra, in a sense, to be Shiva, and trusts the fierce one has a gentle face. Here's the teaching, and a practice you can still watch: Hindus chant the Rudram at abhishekam, as water or milk is poured slowly over the Shiva linga, on Mondays, Shiva's day, and through the night of Shivaratri. Many devotees speak of the pouring as cooling and soothing the fierce one, the way the gods once calmed him with the hymn. Facing anger, there are two easy moves: pretend it isn't there, or go to war with it. The Rudram does neither. It bows, sees the anger fully, and from that bow asks for peace. The hymn says that works on a god. It's worth trying on a temper too, including your own.

segments.voice: Try a small abhishekam. If you have a Shiva linga or an image, pour a little water over it slowly; if not, pour water from one cup into another. As it flows, let something that angers you come to mind, yours or someone else's, and see it clearly without fighting it. If you pray, say namaste rudra manyave, or Om namah shivaya. If you don't, ask the anger, silently, for its kinder face.
The Rudram. A Vedic hymn offered to calm the archer born of wrath: it bows to his anger and asks him to be shiva, kind.

segments.voice: In Ujjain, the Shiva Purana says, King Chandrasena worships Shiva as Mahakala, the great lord of time, with all the splendor a king can offer. A cowherd's little boy watches. He goes home, finds a plain stone, sets it up, and worships it the way he saw the king do, with leaves and whatever he has. His mother, tired of it, throws the stone away. The boy cries until he falls asleep. When he wakes, a shining shrine stands where his stone had been.
screen: `A KING WORSHIPS MAHAKALA.` → `A COWHERD'S BOY, A PLAIN STONE.` → `A SHINING SHRINE.`

segments.voice: Ujjain's Mahakala is still one of the twelve jyotirlingas, the great shrines of Shiva as light, and this story belongs to it: a child with no priest and no Sanskrit. The Rudram said it first. Still in its opening section, it points to a figure crossing the sky, copper, red, brown, wholly auspicious, the blue-throated one, glowing. Then the surprising line. The cowherds have seen him. The women carrying water have seen him. All beings have seen him. May he, seen, be kind to us. Some readers, following the old commentary of Sayana, take that figure as the sun. On that reading, Rudra isn't locked away in a temple or a cave. He's in plain view every morning, and the first people the hymn names as having seen him aren't sages or kings. They're a cowherd and a woman fetching water, in the middle of their work. Here's the Hindu teaching under both: Shiva is seen by everyone, not only priests. Temples have priests and rules, and Hindus value them. But the one worshipped there isn't hidden from anyone who looks. It's why so many Hindus keep a small shrine at home, why a stone under a tree can be a place of worship, and why the morning offering of water to the rising sun needs no one's permission. So when someone asks if they're allowed to come, if they're Hindu enough, if they know enough Sanskrit, the hymn has already answered. The cowherds have seen him.
screen: `MAHAKALA, A JYOTIRLINGA.` · `THE COWHERDS HAVE SEEN HIM.` · `SEEN, MAY HE BE KIND.` · `A SHRINE AT HOME, A STONE BY A TREE.` · then, large: `SEEN BY EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Do what many Hindus do at sunrise, with whatever light you have. Face a window or a lamp, hold a cup of water, and pour a little out slowly, into a plant or a bowl, as an offering to the light. Remember the cowherd's boy with his stone, and the women carrying water. If you pray, say Om namah shivaya, or greet the light as the hymn does. If you don't, just look, and let looking be enough.

segments.voice: Gunanidhi was a learned man's son who became a gambler and a thief, and was thrown out of his home. On Shivaratri night, the Shiva Purana says, he crept, starving, into a Shiva temple, where devotees had left food and fallen asleep. The lamp was going out. So he could see to steal, he tore a strip from his cloth, made a new wick and turned the flame up bright. He grabbed the food, someone woke, he ran, and that night he was killed.
screen: `A THIEF ON SHIVARATRI NIGHT.` → `A DYING LAMP, TURNED UP.` → `HE RUNS, AND DIES.`

segments.voice: Then the story turns. Death's messengers come for him, and Shiva's own attendants stop them. Without meaning to, Gunanidhi had fasted, kept awake and kept Shiva's lamp burning on Shivaratri. He's born again as a king who lights lamps in Shiva's temples, and in time, the Purana says, becomes Kubera, the lord of wealth, Shiva's friend. Now listen to the sound the Rudram keeps making. Namo, namah, like a drumbeat. Namah means a bow; it's the word inside namaste. Line after line of the Namakam is built the same way: namah, a name of Rudra, often cha, and. And look who gets the bow. Carpenters and potters. Hunters, and dogs, and the keepers of dogs. And yes, the line says it: a bow to the lord of thieves. The Rudram isn't praising stealing. It's saying there's no corner where Shiva isn't, so there's no one the bow skips. That's a core Hindu teaching, and you can see it in the most ordinary gesture: palms together, a small bow, namaste. Many Hindus explain it as bowing to the divine in the other person. A thief in a dark temple was still close enough to Shiva to turn up his light. So when someone cuts the line, snaps at you, takes what isn't theirs, the hymn doesn't say it's fine. It says they're not outside the bow. Namah. I see you there, and I bow.
screen: `SHIVA'S ATTENDANTS CLAIM HIM.` · `NAMAH: A BOW, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `EVEN THE LORD OF THIEVES.` · `NAMASTE: THE DIVINE IN YOU.` · then, large: `NO ONE OUTSIDE THE BOW.`

segments.voice: Put your palms together at your chest, the gesture of namaste. Bring to mind people from your week, one at a time: someone you love, someone you barely noticed, someone who annoyed you. For each, bow your head a little and say namah, silently. If you pray, end with Om namah shivaya. If you don't, end with the meaning: I see you there, and I bow.
The Rudram. Today's word inside it: namah, a bow, said again and again until no one is left out, not even the lord of thieves.
